summary: Modular monolith Django on DigitalOcean Droplet + Docker Compose with PostgreSQL as the database in EU; front end: Next.js, React Native.

architecture_rationale.text: One Django deployable split into internal modules: clear boundaries for 3 engineers without the operational cost of microservices. Microservices rejected: 3 engineer(s) cannot absorb their operational overhead.

frontend.justification: Web: One React codebase gives SSR/SSG pages for SEO and app-style screens. Fit for this project: team.languages includes JavaScript/TypeScript; strong time to market, which you rated 5/5; well suited to marketplace projects; seo_critical=true and it serves pre-rendered HTML. Mobile: Builds Android and iOS apps from one TypeScript/JavaScript codebase. Fit for this project: team.languages includes JavaScript/TypeScript; strong time to market, which you rated 5/5; JavaScript is listed first (treated as the team's primary language); well suited to marketplace projects.

alternatives.why_not: Lower overall fit: the chosen option wins on project.type (well suited to marketplace projects).
Lower overall fit: limited camera/GPS access.

tradeoffs: App Router and server/client component split add conceptual weight.
Best features assume a Node/serverless host; static export loses SSR.
JS runtime adds memory overhead on very low-end phones.
Some native modules need a development build.

backend.justification: Ships auth, admin panel, ORM and migrations out of the box. Fit for this project: team.languages includes Python; strong time to market, which you rated 5/5; well suited to marketplace projects; built-in admin/back-office screens. Margin: the full stack scores 0.2 fit points above the best stack built on NestJS.

database.choice: PostgreSQL (in Docker Compose on the VM)
database.justification: ACID transactions, JSONB, full-text search, PostGIS and pgvector in one engine. Fit for this project: ACID transactions keep bookings and payouts consistent; well suited to marketplace projects; strong time to market, which you rated 5/5; strong cost, which you rated 4/5. Data stays in FRA1 Frankfurt to satisfy data_residency=eu. Margin: the full stack scores 1.9 fit points above the best stack built on MySQL.

alternatives.choice: MySQL (in Docker Compose on the VM)
alternatives.why_not: Lower overall fit: the chosen option wins on project.type (well suited to marketplace projects).

alternatives.why_not: Lower overall fit: time-series extension adds operations without a time-series need; the chosen option wins on project.type (well suited to marketplace projects).

alternatives.choice: SQL Server / Azure SQL Database (in Docker Compose on the VM)
alternatives.why_not: Lower overall fit: SQL Server licensing and tooling only pay off for .NET teams or existing SQL Server estates; weaker cost, which you rated 4/5.
Excluded: Cloud Firestore is not suited to deployment_model=self_hosted_cloud_vm (infrastructure.deployment_model).

tradeoffs: Horizontal write scaling needs partitioning, read replicas or Citus.

hosting.justification: Cheapest predictable compute; everything in one Compose file. Fit for this project: matches deployment_model=self_hosted_cloud_vm; strong cost, which you rated 4/5; strong time to market, which you rated 5/5.

alternatives.why_not: Lower overall fit: starts around $250/month against a $150 budget; Kubernetes is over-engineering for 3 engineers at this scale; a large amount of infrastructure to operate with no DevOps engineer.
Excluded: Azure Static Web Apps is not suited to deployment_model=self_hosted_cloud_vm (infrastructure.deployment_model).

tradeoffs: You patch the OS, run backups and handle failover yourself.
A fair amount of infrastructure to operate with no DevOps engineer.

supporting.justification: Uses the backend framework's maintained auth library, so user data stays in your own database in EU. OTPs are sent through Twilio Verify.

alternatives.why_not: Separate vendor with per-MAU pricing.
Firebase Authentication processes data in the US.

tradeoffs: Account recovery and MFA flows must still be designed.

supporting.justification: Collects from buyers, splits the platform fee and pays out to sellers' connected accounts, with KYC for sellers handled by Stripe.

alternatives.why_not: Enterprise onboarding and minimums.
Weaker payout control.

tradeoffs: Gateway fees (~2% per transaction) are not part of the infra estimate.

supporting.justification: Clients upload directly with pre-signed URLs, so large files never pass through the API; objects are encrypted at rest and private by default.

alternatives.why_not: Another vendor and egress fees.

tradeoffs: Needs lifecycle rules to control growth.

supporting.justification: Caches public pages and media close to users and absorbs traffic spikes. Private user uploads bypass the CDN and are served via short-lived signed links from the bucket in the residency region.

alternatives.why_not: Slower first loads for public pages and media.

supporting.justification: Runs inside the existing backend; a Redis adapter lets several instances share connections.

alternatives.why_not: Per-connection pricing for something the backend can do itself.

tradeoffs: Long-lived connections must be drained on deploys; size Redis pub/sub for peak fan-out.

supporting.justification: Caches hot reads and sessions to hold p95=500ms, and carries pub/sub for real-time fan-out.

alternatives.why_not: No pub/sub or persistence, so it cannot double as a broker.
Every read hits the database at peak.

tradeoffs: Another stateful component to size and monitor.

supporting.justification: Moves slow or retry-prone work (payment webhooks, image/file processing, notifications) off the request path so p95 stays low and failures retry safely.

alternatives.why_not: Event-streaming platform: heavy to run for job queues at this scale.

tradeoffs: Jobs must be idempotent; monitor the dead-letter queue.

supporting.choice: PostgreSQL full-text search (tsvector + GIN, pg_trgm for typos)
supporting.justification: At 30000 users and ~50 GB the database's own search is fast enough, transactional and needs no sync pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Better typo tolerance and ranking, but another service to keep in sync; move to it if search becomes core.
Over-sized at this scale.

supporting.justification: Free push delivery to Android for booking and job-status updates. Android push always goes through FCM; payloads carry only an ID and a short text, never personal data, so residency is unaffected.

alternatives.why_not: Costs per message and DLT templates.

tradeoffs: Notification payloads must not contain sensitive data.

supporting.choice: GitHub Actions + Expo EAS (Build, Submit, Update)
supporting.justification: Runs tests and deploys on every merge; free minutes cover a small team. EAS builds signed Android/iOS binaries in the cloud, submits them to the stores and ships JavaScript-only fixes over the air.

alternatives.why_not: Self-hosted server to maintain.

supporting.justification: Free Developer plan catches errors in the backend and mobile apps with stack traces.

alternatives.why_not: Strong product but expensive per host at this budget.

assumptions: Scale level L2: ~30000 users, ~800 peak concurrent, ~160 req/s at peak, ~50 GB stored
SMS OTP: ~$0.001-0.004 per user per month (OTP only on new devices/expired sessions, ~$0.002-0.005 per SMS)
Upper bound capped at ~3x the lower bound: components do not all reach their peak tier in the same month, so the per-line maxima in the breakdown are not meant to add up to the total
List prices for the smallest production tier that fits; no reserved-instance or startup credits; excludes domains, app-store fees and payment-gateway transaction fees

warnings.message: The low estimate ($56) fits the $150 budget, but the upper estimate ($218) exceeds it as usage grows; set billing alerts and use the cost-control notes in each component.
Taking payments: use the gateway's hosted checkout/SDK so card data never touches your servers (PCI DSS SAQ A).
